models.approach: Argue from access for the people who currently get least, then concede what an examination requires.
plan: Introduction: what telemedicine changes, and where you land.
Body 1: advantages, access, time and cost.
Body 2: disadvantages, examination, exclusion and continuity.
Conclusion: the verdict and the sorting rule it implies.

paras.text: Consulting a doctor by video has moved in a few years from an experiment to an ordinary appointment. It brings clear gains and equally clear limits, and [[on balance]] I believe the advantages outweigh the drawbacks, provided the system knows which patients it is unsuitable for.

The largest benefit is reach. A patient two hours from the nearest clinic, or one who cannot leave work without losing pay, can now be seen at all, and for them the alternative was not a worse consultation but none. Specialist opinion travels the same way: a rural doctor can consult a consultant in a city the same afternoon, which [[expedites|Expedite]] diagnosis considerably. [[It is worth noting]] that the saving in clinic time is [[invaluable]] to systems with long waiting lists, since a video appointment occupies no room.

[[By contrast]], a camera cannot palpate an abdomen or smell an infection, and a doctor deprived of those signs is working with [[deficient]] information. The risk is not a missed cold but a missed cancer. Access is also uneven: the elderly and the poorest are least likely to have a decent connection or a private room, which means the format can widen the gap it was meant to close. [[Regrettably]], continuity suffers too, as many services rotate whichever clinician is free.

[[Taken together]], telemedicine is a genuine advance for the ordinary consultation and a poor substitute for the difficult one. The [[pragmatic]] arrangement is a triage rule: video for review, results and medication, and a room for anything undiagnosed, with a telephone alternative for patients without the technology.

notes: The alternative was not a worse consultation but none is the sentence that decides this essay. State what the comparison actually is.
Both paragraphs name who is affected rather than describing the technology, which keeps the essay on the human consequences.
The conclusion is a rule that could be written into a policy, which is a stronger finish than a balance of sentiment.

models.approach: Argue that the gains are real for the simple case and that health systems are applying it to the hard one.
plan: Introduction: concede the convenience, question where it is being used.
Body 2: disadvantages, diagnosis, equity and the erosion of the relationship.
Conclusion: what should be kept and what abandoned.

paras.text: Remote consultation is convenient, cheap for the provider and popular with the healthy. [[In my opinion]] those three facts explain its spread better than any clinical evidence, and the disadvantages outweigh the benefits as it is currently being deployed.

[[It is true that]] the benefits are genuine for straightforward matters. Repeat prescriptions, test results and mental health follow-ups work perfectly well on a screen, and for a patient in a remote district the arrangement is [[indispensable]]. [[For the most part]], patients also report high satisfaction, though satisfaction and accuracy are not the same measurement.

[[Nevertheless]], the format is being extended to first presentations, which is where the danger sits. Examination is how most serious disease is caught early, and a consultation without it relies on the patient describing what they do not know is significant. [[There is evidence that]] remote triage delays some cancer diagnoses by months. The relationship suffers too: a doctor who has never met a patient cannot notice that they look worse than last year, and that [[intuitive]] comparison is a real diagnostic instrument. [[Not surprisingly]], the patients most harmed are the old, the poor and those whose first language is not the doctor's.

[[All things considered]], telemedicine should be a supplement rather than a default. Keeping it for follow-up and remote regions while restoring face-to-face access for anything new would preserve the benefits, whereas the present direction [[jeopardizes|Jeopardize]] the early diagnosis that health systems depend on.

notes: Satisfaction and accuracy are not the same measurement is a single sentence that undercuts the strongest evidence for the other side.
Naming who is harmed most keeps the essay from being a general complaint about technology.
A supplement rather than a default is a precise verdict, and the conclusion says exactly which uses survive.

models.approach: Sort consultations into those that are speech and those that require a body in a room.
plan: Introduction: the format is neither good nor bad; the consultation decides.
Body 1: consultations that are essentially conversation.
Body 2: consultations that are essentially examination.
Conclusion: the sorting rule and who should apply it.

paras.text: Whether telemedicine helps or harms depends on something the debate usually skips: what the appointment actually consists of. [[To a certain extent]] both camps are right, because they are describing different consultations.

A great deal of medicine is talking. Reviewing a chronic condition, adjusting a dose, delivering a normal result and most psychological therapy are conducted almost entirely in speech, and for these the screen removes travel and waiting without removing anything clinical. [[A case in point]] is talking therapy, where completion rates rose when sessions moved online because attendance no longer required an afternoon off. [[Broadly speaking]], the advantages here are [[irrefutable]].

[[By contrast]], a first presentation of an unexplained symptom is not a conversation. The doctor is gathering signs the patient cannot report, and removing that is not a small compromise but the removal of the method itself. Digital exclusion compounds it: the patients with the most complex needs are the least likely to manage the technology, so the format is [[insidious]] in sorting patients by their equipment rather than their illness.

[[On the whole]], then, the question is not whether to use telemedicine but who decides which appointments it suits. That judgement belongs to a clinician rather than a booking system, and where it has been handed to the booking system the disadvantages have been [[pervasive]].

notes: Sorting by what the consultation consists of gives the two paragraphs a clean, non-overlapping division.
The therapy example includes a mechanism, no afternoon off, which explains why the advantage exists rather than asserting it.
Locating the real question in who decides is a genuine conclusion rather than a restatement.
